Signal a typed error the caller may recover from. The payload is a domain-specific error `data`
(e.g. `json.parse_error`); a handler at that payload type catches it — `use handler { request
throw(error: my_error) -> never { break fallback } }` — and an unhandled throw fails the run with
the payload. `-> never` means a throw cannot be resumed: a handler recovers by `break`ing out of
the handle (or rethrows).

block.description:
Run @task@ and fold its `throw` into the RESULT: the answer is @task@'s value, or — when it threw —
the thrown payload itself, as a plain `T | Err` union to `match` on. This is the ONE general way a
program turns the error CHANNEL into an error VALUE, and it exists because the hand-written form is
four lines of ceremony whose only variation is a type name: install a handler, `break` the payload out
of the handle, and re-spell the payload type twice. Written `catch(task = agent () -> ... { ... })`,
the whole thing is one expression.

WHAT IT REPLACES, and why they are gone: a total twin of a throwing reader (`json.try_validate` beside
`json.validate`), a bulk pre-check that folds every failure to a boolean (`credentials.check`), a
`_as`-suffixed variant that validates a request's answer — each was the same fold, specialised once per
call site. One general form means the composition is written where it is needed, in the caller's own
words, instead of being anticipated per operation.

IT CATCHES THE WHOLE THROW ROW, not a chosen part of it: the row is `E lacks prelude.throw`, so
whatever @task@ can throw comes back as @Err@ and nothing throwing survives into @catch@'s own row.
Partial capture — catch these payloads, let the rest keep flying — is NOT expressible here and stays a
hand-written handler with a rethrow arm, because the union would have to be split against a rigid type
variable. That is the deliberate line: `catch` is for the boundary where a failure BECOMES data, a
handler is for the boundary where a failure is REROUTED.

TWO THINGS TO KNOW. A @task@ that throws NOTHING leaves @Err@ with no lower bound and fails to infer
(K3016) — write `catch[T, never]` if you really mean it, though catching a task that cannot throw says
nothing worth saying. And the answer is a bare union, so an instantiation where @T@ and @Err@ OVERLAP
cannot tell the two apart afterwards — the ordinary shapes do not (a value and a `data` error are
structurally disjoint), but a `catch[unknown, ...]` deliberately blurs them.

task.description: The work to run; its throws are folded into the result. Written inline as an anonymous nullary agent (`agent () -> T with ... { ... }`) — the `(value: null)` here is the accepting bound, not a shape to imitate.

block.description:
The SHA-256 digest of @text@'s UTF-8 bytes, as 64 lowercase hex characters. Deterministic and pure,
so a replay recomputes the same digest. Typical uses: a content dedupe key, or a stable tag for an
external identifier — but note that a plain digest of an ENUMERABLE input (a numeric user id, an
email) is reversible by dictionary: anyone can hash every candidate and match. For a tag that must
not be reversible, use `hmac_sha256` with a secret key. Takes PUBLIC text only — hashing a secret
would raise a declassification question (is the digest of a secret still secret?) that this plain
digest deliberately leaves unanswered; `hmac_sha256` answers it for the keyed form.

text.description: The text to digest, hashed as its UTF-8 bytes.

block.description:
The HMAC-SHA-256 tag of @text@ under the secret @key@, as 64 lowercase hex characters — the
IRREVERSIBLE tag `sha256` cannot give over an enumerable input: without the key a dictionary attack
is impossible, so hashing a user id with a secret key yields a pseudonym that is stable for one key
and opaque to everyone without it (a chat bot's abuse-attribution tag is the canonical use; rotating
the key rotates every pseudonym). The result is deliberately PUBLIC despite the private key: an HMAC
tag reveals nothing about the key by construction — irreversibility IS the sound declassification —
so this is the one prim whose result the runtime does not taint private. Deterministic, so a replay
recomputes the same tag.

key.description: The secret key material; the tag is stable per key and unforgeable without it.

text.description: The text to tag, as its UTF-8 bytes; public, like `sha256`'s.

block.description:
A short, STABLE, IRREVERSIBLE stand-in for @value@ under the secret @key@ — the first @length@ hex
characters of its HMAC-SHA-256 tag. The same value under the same key always yields the same
pseudonym, two different values effectively never collide at the default width, and nobody without
the key can go backwards or forwards: they can neither read the original out of the tag nor check a
guess against it.

This is two lines over `hmac_sha256` and it is here for WHICH two lines. The thing being pseudonymised
is always an identifier — a chat user id, an email address, an account number — and an identifier is
ENUMERABLE, which is exactly the input a plain `sha256` fails on: anyone can hash every candidate id
and match the digest, so the "anonymous" tag names its subject to the first person who tries. The
composition that reaches for `sha256` is short, natural, and wrong, and it is wrong SILENTLY — the
output looks identical. Encoding the keyed choice in the name is the point; the slicing is incidental.

@length@ is a collision / brevity trade, not a security one (truncating an HMAC does not make it
reversible): 8 hex characters distinguish on the order of tens of thousands of subjects before a
birthday collision is likely, which is the scale of a chat community. Widen it for a bigger population.
ROTATING THE KEY ROTATES EVERY PSEUDONYM — that is the erasure story, and the reason the key belongs in
the project's secret env rather than in the source. The result is PUBLIC despite the private key, for
`hmac_sha256`'s reason: irreversibility IS the sound declassification, so a pseudonym may be shown to a
model, written to a store, or rendered into a message.

key.description: The secret key the pseudonym is stable under; rotating it rotates every pseudonym.

length.description: How many hex characters to keep; a collision / brevity trade, not a security one.

value.description: The identifier to stand in for — a user id, an address; public, and enumerable, which is why the tag is keyed.

read surface, and TOTAL by construction: an unset knob is not a failure, so there is nothing to catch and
nothing to branch on. @fallback@ is the value the program means when nobody configured one, which is a

check (`get_or(key = ..., fallback = "") == ""`) deliberately does not.

block.description:
Perform an HTTP request to @url@ with @method@, the given @headers@ and @body@ — EXACTLY `fetch`'s
request — but capture the RESPONSE body as a downloaded `file` rather than as text. The bytes land in the
blob store and the reply carries only the slim @file@ HANDLE; the raw bytes (and their base64) never touch
the value plane, the durable call record, or the trace. This is the receive-side twin of a `binary`
REQUEST body, and it exists for the same reason: to keep a payload's bytes OFF the value plane. A plain
`fetch` of a megabyte image would read it into the response `body` STRING, dragging that text (and its
base64, once re-encoded) through every value, event, and trace it flows into — whereas `fetch_file` streams
it straight to a blob and hands back a handle. Reach for it to download a file by URL: an image, a PDF, a
CSV export, a release artifact. It is NOT for a base64 field buried inside a JSON reply (a data-URI in an
API's JSON document) — `fetch_file` only ever captures the WHOLE response body; decode an embedded base64
string with `files.from_base64` after an ordinary `fetch`. The downloaded @file@'s recorded content type is
the response's `Content-Type` (falling back to `application/octet-stream` when the server sent none).
Returns the response @status@ code (branch on it exactly like `fetch` — a non-2xx reply's body is still
captured to a @file@, so a caller inspects @status@ before trusting the download), its @headers@ (names
lowercased; repeated headers joined with ", "), and the downloaded @file@. A request that never completes
throws `fetch_error`, exactly like `fetch`.

block.description:
POST @body@ — a JSON value tree — to @url@ as application/json with the given @headers@, and return the
reply PARSED into its document value. This is the canonical one-call shape of a JSON API integration: build
the body as an ordinary record / array / scalar tree, post it, and read the reply as a value — no manual
`json.stringify` / `json.parse` around the call. @body@ AND each header value may be a secret (an auth token
— an "Authorization" of "Bearer <key>" for OpenAI, an "x-goog-api-key" for Gemini — or a `refresh_token`
in the body of an OAuth exchange): both are submitted only to @url@'s server, which stays public. A `file`
placed anywhere in @body@ rides as base64 (the `http.json` slot contract). The Content-Type defaults to
application/json unless a header overrides it.

A NON-2xX IS CLASSIFIED HERE, not merely reported: it throws `api_failure` — `auth_error` for 401 / 403,
`api_error` for everything else — carrying the status, @context@ and the server's own body. That is the
whole reason this wrapper takes a @context@: a thrown failure travels away from its call site, so WHICH
call failed has to ride with it, in the caller's own words ("tavily.search", "gmail.send"), and a human
or a model reading the error gets both halves without a renderer splitting a sentence.

Classifying HERE rather than at the caller is what keeps the vocabulary single. A raw "non-2xx" error type
alongside `api_failure` meant the same fact wore two types — every package that wanted a retry policy or a
re-auth converter re-classified the first into the second, in a shim that was the same three lines each
time and had to be remembered. There is now one type for a rejected call, produced in one place, and the
status rides on it so a downstream policy reads a NUMBER (408 / 429 / 5xx are worth repeating) instead of
searching an English sentence.

A transport failure throws `fetch_error`; a 2xx body that is not JSON throws `json.parse_error` (a JSON API
that broke its promise) — an empty 2xx body is `null`. To send already-serialized text, to keep the raw
reply text, or to branch on a status rather than throw on it, call `fetch` directly.

block.description:
Classify a non-2xx @status@ into the shared vocabulary: 401 and 403 are `auth_error` (a credential
problem no retry with the same credential can fix), EVERY other status is `api_error`. @context@ and
@message@ ride onto whichever variant comes out, unchanged.

This is the ONE place the line is drawn, and that is the point. The classification used to be re-decided
per package — `gmail`, `google_calendar`, `tavily` and every OAuth REST integration written after them each
carried a private copy of the same two-arm `match`, so "Google's 401" and "Anthropic's 401" wore
different types and an app composing two of them wrote one `supervise` converter per package to say the same
thing twice. With one classifier the vocabulary is one vocabulary: a converter matches `http.auth_error`
once and covers every API behind it.

The STATUS IS RETAINED on the way out, deliberately. A caller downstream decides whether to back off and
repeat (408 / 429 / 5xx) or to give up (a 400 the service is refusing), and that decision is a number
comparison on `api_error.status` — never a substring search through a human sentence, which is what the
statusless vocabulary forced. Reach for this at the ONE boundary where a package reads its responses; it
answers a VALUE, so the caller chooses whether to throw it, fold it, or attach it to an outcome.

block.description:
Open an MCP server connection for the extent of @continuation@ WITHOUT listing the server — the
listing-free form of `provide`, same scoped contract, no toolbox. The runtime registers the
connection's `Scope` (minted for @continuation@'s row, DISCHARGED from `open`'s own — exactly
`provide`'s rule, so a live tool context still cannot be forged) and starts @continuation@
immediately with `null`: no server round-trip happens at open, and the connection tears down when
@continuation@ settles (or the run is cancelled). Tools are reached STATICALLY through
`mcp.call[Scope, T]` under the same `{url, auth}` descriptor — the shape a `katari mcp pull` binding
generates — so prefer `open` wherever the toolbox would be ignored: a pulled binding's `connect`,
and per-call connections, where `provide`'s per-open listing is pure overhead. `provide` remains the
dynamic-toolbox form (list the server, hand runtime-minted tools to an AI loop). Because nothing is
contacted at open, auth surfaces at the FIRST `mcp.call`: a missing or dead `oauth` credential
pauses that call on an authorization escalation, and rejected `headers` material / server failures
are its typed throws.

block.description:
Plug an MCP server's tools into a program for the extent of @continuation@, as a scoped provider —
the `use mcp.provide(url = ..., auth = ...)` form. The runtime lists the server (a missing or dead
`oauth` credential pauses on an authorization escalation and retries once answered; rejected `headers`
material throws `auth_error`; a rejected listing throws `server_error`), hands @continuation@
a `toolbox[Scope]` of one runtime-minted agent per tool (each carrying the server signature — for
`reflection.get_metadata` and call-site validation — and the descriptor it was listed with), and settles
with the continuation's result. `Scope` rides the continuation's row (that is what a tool call raises) and
is DISCHARGED from `provide`'s own row, so a tool cannot escape the block: the scope closes when
@continuation@ returns (or the run is cancelled), and a stray later call is rejected as a typed
`server_error`. `Scope` is the marker the tools are gated by — the built-in `mcp.scope` for the dynamic
path, or a generated binding's module-local marker; pass it explicitly as the first `[...]` argument
(`mcp.provide[mcp.scope](...)`), and the toolbox binder's annotation must agree. Discharging `Scope` is
`provide`'s alone (only it opens the connection), so a live tool context cannot be forged. @url@ is a plain
routing value: the runtime connects and caches under the `{url, auth}` descriptor.
DECLARE ONE MARKER PER LOGICAL CONNECTION. When you call `provide` directly you choose `Scope` yourself:
share ONE marker across two connections and their scopes MERGE at the type level (the two servers' tools
become mutually substitutable in a row that carries the marker) — the same widening the old dynamic-URL
`toolbox[string]` had, no worse. It is only a TYPE distinction: routing and the live-`provide` backstop are
always enforced by each tool value's own `{url, auth}` descriptor, so a call never reaches the wrong
server — at worst a tool whose `provide` has closed fails with a typed `server_error`. A `katari mcp pull`
binding needs no such discipline: its module namespace mints a distinct marker (`github.connection`) per
connection automatically, so pulled servers never share a scope. When the toolbox itself is never read —
a pulled binding's tools call through the static `mcp.call` — `open` is the listing-free form of this
same contract.

anyOf.description:
seen_set: Dedup by a BOUNDED SET OF KEYS — for a source with no usable receive clock, only a window that
slides ("meetings starting within the next 30 minutes"). No cursor moves; every fetch sees the same
`since` and works from the tick instant instead. The memory is the most recent @capacity@ keys.

A CAP IS NOT A PRUNE TO THE CURRENT WINDOW — that is trap 4, and it is why this is a cap. THE
RE-NOTIFY HAZARD IT LEAVES: forgetting the oldest key means an item that is STILL inside the window
after @capacity@ other items have been delivered will be delivered again. Size @capacity@ well above
the largest number of items one window can hold (google_calendar uses 200 for a 30-minute lead) and
the drop only ever reaches keys long past; size it too small and a busy window re-notifies its own
head. There is no cheaper bound — the memory has to forget something, and age is the only safe axis.

A SEEN-SET SUBSCRIPTION CANNOT BACKFILL, whatever its `continuity`: with no floor there is nothing to
list from, so whatever crossed the window while the subscription was down is simply gone. `resume`
still earns its keep here — it stops the re-notification storm a re-primed memory would cause — but
only a `watermark` subscription delivers its downtime.

anyOf.description:

composes under `parallel [ … ]` beside any other daemon and beside other subscriptions.

DELIVERY IS AT-LEAST-ONCE. An item reaches @deliver_to@ one or more times, never zero: the commit lands
only after a delivery returns, so a crash or a throw in between re-delivers exactly that item on the
next tick. Build exactly-once at the DESTINATION by making the delivery idempotent — keyed by
`item.key`, which is the identity this loop already promises is stable.

WHAT @fetch@ MUST GUARANTEE, and it is the whole adapter: given @since@ (the instant this tick lists
from — the cursor's floor minus the regime's overlap) and @tick@ (the occurrence's scheduled instant),
return every item at or above @since@, OLDEST FIRST, across every page of the source's pagination.
Oldest-first is load-bearing: the cursor then only ever passes items that have actually been
delivered, so a delivery that throws mid-tick leaves the rest of the tick still above the cursor.
Draining every page is load-bearing too: a listing cut off at a cap that orders newest-first hands
back only the newest matches, and a cursor advanced over them strands the older ones below it forever.
Returning an item AGAIN that was returned before is free — that is what the remembered keys are for.

WHAT IT REPORTS. With `skip_backlog` it reports ARRIVALS: whatever the source already held when the
subscription first started is never delivered, however well it matches, and an old item that comes to
match LATER is not delivered either (the fetch never looks below the cursor). That is the right shape
for hearing about new things and the wrong one for "tell me whenever anything matches"; a listing
agent answers the latter.

re-forked fiber and a `supervise` re-run all RESUME from it — and the items that arrived while the
subscription was down are delivered, oldest first, on the tick after it comes back. With `fresh()`
every activation re-primes and that downtime is skipped for good. Nothing else about the subscription
changes between the two.

as an uncaught failure in any callee does. Compose resilience at the call site: `supervise.forever` plus a
converter that turns the transient failures (and, for an OAuth source, `auth_error`) into
`supervise.interrupted`. With `resume`, the backoff costs nothing but latency; the cursor survives it.

start), and under `seen_set` + `skip_backlog` that first poll is the priming one — so the earliest
notification such a subscription can produce is two occurrences after it starts.

block.description: The nursery's WHITE HOLE: re-emit the fibers' escalations into the enclosing program as the ceiling effect `E`, plus the runtime's own `crashed` and `failed` events. It returns `never` — it only ever raises, never yields — so install a `handler` (or any row that covers `E | crashed | failed`) around it to service the fibers' requests. Because every fiber's effect fits under `E` and `watch` re-emits the FULL `E`, covering `E | crashed | failed` here covers everything any fiber can surface. This is the ONE channel out of a fiber: a normal completion is silent (the settled `null` is discarded — a task that has something to say says it as its last act), a cancellation is silent (the canceller knows), and the TWO endings a task cannot report itself arrive as typed events — a PANIC as `crashed`, an uncaught `prelude.throw` as `failed`. In both the runtime tears the ended fiber down and reports the ending as data, so what a death MEANS is your handler's decision, not an unwinding accident; and because the throw is trapped HERE, no `fork` has to wrap its task in a throw guard just to keep the region standing. Scope-gated (`with Scope`): callable only inside the opening `provide`. A fiber may escalate BEFORE any `watch` is installed (it forks, then waits on an FFI / http / AI call, and the watch is set up only later): every such escalation is held DURABLY and re-emitted the moment a `watch` registers, in arrival order — so a watch installed arbitrarily late still receives every earlier escalation, and a fiber need not delay its first raise until a watch is up. WATCH IS TRANSPARENT — IT IMPOSES NO SERIALIZATION OF ITS OWN. It re-emits EVERY fiber escalation CONCURRENTLY, the moment it arrives, so the ONLY serialization point is the RECEIVING handler: a sequential (stateful `var`) handler serializes its OWN invocations at its FIFO, in ARRIVAL order, while a `parallel handler` runs them concurrently. ONE watch is enough: it interleaves every fiber's stream by construction — do NOT run several to gain concurrency (the concurrency is already there; the desks are told apart by their handlers, not by extra watches).

block.description:
Run @task@ as a CRITICAL SECTION of the nearest enclosing `workspace`: the workspace's SEQUENTIAL
handler calls it in its own body, so two exclusives of one domain can never interleave — the
handler's FIFO is the atomicity, even against a `parallel for` tool batch. The row is FIXED to the
store operations: a critical section reads, computes and writes, NOTHING ELSE — any other input is
computed BEFORE entering and closed over — so a section can never block on a model, a network, or
another domain. TWO GEOMETRY FACTS, both load-bearing: the task runs AT THE WORKSPACE INSTALL SITE,
not at this perform site — so a facility's subdirectory prefix must be applied INSIDE the task body
(`use store.workspace(path = "memory")` as the task's first move; a workspace around the perform
site does not travel with the task, but the install site's own enclosing workspaces do apply). And an
`exclusive` binds to the NEAREST enclosing workspace: an inner domain shadows an outer one BY DESIGN
— the nearest domain is the semantics, exactly as the nearest prefix is. The task's answer crosses
the handler as `unknown`; narrow it back with a `match` (or `json.validate[T]`). With NO workspace
installed above the perform, the RUNTIME serves it as the outermost domain — the task runs at the
PROJECT ROOT (project-root keys) in one durable, project-wide FIFO across every run.

block.description:
Open the WORKSPACE at @path@ under the current one, for the extent of @continuation@ — the
`use store.workspace(path = "core")` form, and the store's ONE provider. It installs both halves of
a working directory:

  - THE PREFIX. Four parallel handlers catch the store operations and RE-PERFORM them outward with
    the prefixed key (`get(key = "index")` under a workspace at "core" escalates as
    `get(key = "core/index")`; a `list` gets @path@ prepended to its own path parameter), so nested
    workspaces accumulate prefixes and the outermost bare perform is project-root access — unhandled
    at the very top, the runtime machine-answers against the project's durable rows. Those four are
    PARALLEL on purpose: prefixing is stateless arithmetic and must not serialize the traffic passing
    through it (a turn's tool batch stays concurrent).
  - THE DOMAIN. One sequential handler serves `exclusive` by calling the section in its own body, so
    the FIFO applies critical sections one at a time, in arrival order — which is the whole point (a
    parallel clause would forfeit the atomicity). Sections re-perform their store operations from
    THIS install site, so they land under THIS workspace's prefix.

The install order between them is fixed here and is not a preference: the prefix handlers sit OUTSIDE
the domain, so a critical section's keys resolve through the workspace it was opened in. A nested
workspace is therefore a nested prefix AND a nested domain, exactly as it reads, and an `exclusive`
performed below it binds to the nearest one.

A workspace is a ONE-WAY DESCENT: there is deliberately no `..`, so data several workspaces share is
NOT reached by path escape — it is reached by a REQUEST served ABOVE the workspaces, whose clause
opens the shared subtree in its own body. That proxy is the semantics: a request is what an inner
install can never capture by accident. `share` / `shared` below is that proxy, generalised once so it
need not be respelt per shared cell.

@path@ is one or more `/`-separated SEGMENTS, each spelled as `safe_segment` requires (lowercase
letters, digits, `-`, `_`). A path that is not — an empty segment, a `..`, a stray space, a name a
model chose and nobody checked — PANICS here rather than opening a workspace somewhere else: the
descent is the program's own geometry, so a malformed one is a defect in the program and not an
outcome a caller could route. Validate a name that came from OUTSIDE the program with `safe_segment`
first, and render its `null` into whatever sentence the proposer should read.

ONE IMPRECISION TO KNOW ABOUT, because it shows up in the escalation report. All five clauses are
installed, and each re-performs its own operation, so this agent's row names all four store
operations whatever the continuation actually does — a caller that only reads still carries `set` and
`delete` outward. The row is sound (a workspace really can perform all four on its continuation's
behalf) but it is coarser than the truth, so the report reads as though a read-only agent could
delete. Narrowing it needs the row to follow which requests the continuation performs, which the
language cannot express yet; until it can, read a workspaced agent's store row as "reaches the
store" rather than as the set of operations it uses.

is ABSENT or holds a value that is not one — the TYPED store read, and the only one a program should
normally write. A stored cell is an `unknown` no schema guards (an older run's shape, a hand edit in the
console, a key another facility took over), so every read is a boundary read: `get` folded through
`json.validate[T]`, with the mismatch folded to @fallback@ by `prelude.catch`. T is read off @fallback@
— a `get_or(key = ..., fallback = 0)` reads an integer, a `get_or(key = ..., fallback = my_state(...))`

value the caller would have had to supply in a `match` anyway.

longer fits is a cell an EARLIER version of the program wrote, and there is nothing a reader can do
about that except start over from a value it does understand. Reach for a bare `get` when a MISSING
entry must be told apart from a WRONG-TYPED one (a first-run branch), or when the mismatch itself must
be reported — `json.validate`'s `validation_error` names the offending path and this agent drops it.

validates) from a mismatch (which does not) — both come back as `null`, and so does an absent key. Where

Run @task@ AT THE NEAREST ENCLOSING `share`'s install site — that site's workspaces, that site's
serial domain — and hand back what it answered: the ONE request by which a desk reaches knowledge
living ABOVE its own workspace. The geometry is `exclusive`'s, and both halves are load-bearing. The
task is a CLOSURE that travels UP and runs THERE, so a workspace around this PERFORM does not travel
with it (the INSTALL site's own enclosing workspaces do apply) — which means a subdirectory of the
shared place is opened INSIDE the task body (`use store.workspace(path = "shared/soul")` as its first
move), and that is exactly what lets one `share` serve every shared cell instead of one named request
per cell. And it binds to the NEAREST enclosing `share`: an inner shared place shadows an outer one BY
DESIGN, the same dynamic-scope rule the nearest workspace follows. The
row is FIXED to the store operations plus `exclusive`: a task reads, computes and writes, and takes
ATOMICITY by wrapping a read-modify-write in `store.exclusive` INSIDE the task — which lands in the
shared place's own serial domain, since that is where the task is running. Nothing else is in the row,
so a shared access can never block on a model, a network or another domain. The answer crosses back as
`unknown`; narrow it with a `match` (or `json.validate[T]`) at the perform site.
Unlike the store's four operations and `exclusive`, this one is NOT runtime-served, deliberately:
there is no project-root shared place, because a shared place is somewhere a program CHOSE and a
forgotten install must never quietly resolve to project-root keys. With no `share` above it a `shared`
rides to the run root as an ordinary unanswered request — the fate of any provider-backed request that
lost its provider — so the real guard is the effect row, which keeps `shared` visible in every
signature between the perform and the install.

arguments, no type arguments: the shared place is WHERE it is installed, exactly as a workspace is). Serves `shared` by calling its task in the clause body, so a task runs HERE — under this site's
workspaces, over this site's serial domain — while the desks below go on opening their own workspaces
per dispatch and reaching nothing of each other's. THE INSTALL DISCIPLINE, in this order: the app's
workspace, then `share`, then the desks (`use store.workspace(path = "assistant")` then
`use store.share`). The order is a CONTRACT, not a habit: a task's row carries `exclusive` and this
provider re-performs it outward, so `share` must sit INSIDE a workspace for a shared critical section
to land in that workspace's domain — which is what the ordinary install order above already gives. The order is legible in the TYPE, not only in prose: install `share` above the domain
instead and its `exclusive` finds nothing to catch it, so `store.exclusive` surfaces in the enclosing
signature and those sections ride to the runtime's project-wide root FIFO — legal, and visibly a
different program. The handler is PARALLEL on purpose: sending a closure upward is not an ordering
decision, and a sequential clause would queue three desks' concurrent reads of the shared place behind
one another for nothing; ordering is `exclusive`'s job here as everywhere, taken INSIDE the task. A
second `share` below this one captures every `shared` under it — the ordinary dynamic-scope rule, and
the way a deliberately NARROWER shared place (a sub-team's own commons, shared among its desks and
invisible to the app's) is expressed. KNOW WHAT THE GENERALISATION COSTS: a request per cell is also a
CAPABILITY per cell — a desk holding `read_digest` and not `save_digest_entry` cannot write the digest
whatever it does — and one `shared` is one capability over the WHOLE shared place. Where a boundary
BETWEEN shared cells is the semantics, keep the named request for that cell; the two compose, since a
named proxy installed below this one can perform `shared` in its own clause.

CUT the string to at most @cap@ code points, and SAY SO when it cut: a value that fits comes back
untouched, and one that does not comes back as its head plus @marker@ — the whole result still at most
@cap@ points, because the marker's own length is taken out of the head first.

This is the one bound every rendered text takes on its way to somewhere with a limit: a chat platform's
per-message ceiling, a tool result a model reads, a summary a store cell holds. The composition
(`slice(value, 0, cap - length(marker)) ++ marker`) is short but it is not SAFE — the arithmetic is
where it goes wrong, and always in the same two ways. Subtracting the marker AFTER slicing overshoots
the cap by exactly the marker (the platform rejects the message, in production, on the one long input
nobody tested), and a @cap@ smaller than the marker makes the slice bound negative, so the truncation
marker alone is the whole answer and it is still too long. Both are silent until the day they are not,
which is what makes this a canonical spelling rather than a shorthand: the judgement being encoded is
`cap` MEANS the whole answer.

A @marker@ that alone exceeds @cap@ is itself cut to @cap@ — the answer is then all marker, which is
the honest reading of a budget too small to say anything in. An empty @marker@ is a plain hard cut, for
a sink whose truncation the reader can already see.
